name: 15. Auth Flaws, Access Control & API Security

quiz.question: An authenticated student requests another student's private report. Which control should decide whether the report can be accessed?
options: The fact that the student has signed in successfully
A server-side object-level authorization check
Whether the report identifier is difficult to guess
A frontend button that hides the report link
quiz.explanation: Authentication confirms identity, but authorization decides if that specific identity owns or has explicit permission to view the resource. A server-side object-level authorization check is required.

quiz.question: What is broken function-level authorization (BFLA)?
options: A user enters an invalid email address
An API returns a temporary network error
A user can invoke an operation that their permissions should not allow
A session expires according to policy
quiz.explanation: Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA, OWASP API5:2023) happens when access control checks are missing on endpoints, allowing regular users or lower-privileged roles to invoke administrative or privileged actions.

quiz.question: Which statement about JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) is correct?
options: A token must have its integrity and required claims validated before it is trusted
A token is trustworthy whenever its payload can be decoded
All JWTs encrypt their claims automatically
An expired token should be accepted if the signature is valid
quiz.explanation: Decoding a JWT payload does not verify its integrity. A resource server must cryptographically verify the signature using an expected algorithm and validate claims like iss, aud, exp, and nbf before trusting it.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of API rate limiting and resource controls?
options: Replace user authentication
Reduce abuse and limit excessive consumption of API and backend resources
Grant every user equal administrative permissions
Eliminate the need for authorization
quiz.explanation: Rate limiting and resource constraints (OWASP API4:2023) protect infrastructure from service degradation, denial-of-service, financial loss from expensive cloud APIs, and automated brute-force attacks.

quiz.question: An ordinary user submits a profile update containing "role": "admin". What is the appropriate control?
options: Accept all model properties automatically
Hide the role field in the frontend only
Restrict writable fields server-side and enforce authorization
Assume the value is safe because it is valid JSON
quiz.explanation: To prevent mass assignment / BOPLA (API3:2023), the backend must explicitly allowlist updateable fields or use a strict Data Transfer Object (DTO), rejecting or ignoring privileged attributes like role.

quiz.question: What is the most appropriate way to handle an API that fetches a URL supplied by a user?
options: Validate and restrict destinations, control redirects, and enforce network egress limits where appropriate
Allow every URL as long as it begins with https://
Disable all certificate validation
Trust the URL because it came through an authenticated user
quiz.explanation: To mitigate Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF, API7:2023), the server must strictly validate destination hostnames/IPs, block RFC1918 private ranges and link-local cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), enforce egress firewall rules, and validate post-redirect destinations.

theorySections.title: Authentication, Authorization, and API Security Fundamentals
paragraphs: Authentication verifies a presented identity claim: "Who are you?" Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a particular operation on a particular resource: "Are you permitted to read or mutate this exact record?"

The login step does not grant blanket permission to every record or endpoint. API authorization must be enforced dynamically when a protected operation is requested, not assumed merely because a request carries a valid session token.

theorySections.title: Authentication Failures and Account Security
paragraphs: Authentication Failure (OWASP Top 10:2025 A07:2025) occurs when an application incorrectly verifies identity or inadequately protects the authentication and credential lifecycle.
Account enumeration occurs when an application reveals whether a particular username or email address exists in the database by returning distinct errors:
"User does not exist" "Incorrect password for user@example.com"
"Invalid email or password. Please verify your credentials."

theorySections.title: Access Control: BOLA, BFLA, and Object Property Authorization
paragraphs: Authorization flaws are among the most prevalent and critical API security weaknesses. OWASP identifies three distinct levels of authorization failure in its API Security Top 10:
Can user Alice read or modify Bob's specific report object just by guessing or tampering with the report ID?
Can a regular user call a function or HTTP method (e.g. DELETE, admin export) reserved for platform administrators?
Can a user read confidential fields (excessive data exposure) or modify restricted fields (mass assignment)?

theorySections.title: Session Security, Tokens, JWTs, and API Credentials
paragraphs: Sessions and tokens act as bearer credentials: whoever possesses the credential can execute operations as the authenticated identity. Insecure handling exposes users to session hijacking and privilege impersonation.
A signed JSON Web Token consists of three base64url-encoded segments separated by periods: header.payload.signature
